1: Open with the core idea: interview preparation is where placements are won or lost. A candidate who walks in underprepared reflects on us, and a client who interviews without being briefed often loses the candidate they wanted. Today covers three things: preparing the candidate, preparing the client, and pre-closing on every call so the offer never comes as a surprise. Ask everyone to have one live interview process in mind; we will use it in the exercises.
2: Open with the line from the original playbook: a candidate who walks in underprepared reflects on us. Ask each person to keep their live candidate in mind and apply every slide to them.
3: Even experienced candidates get the basics wrong under pressure: the wrong office, a camera left off, an outfit that doesn’t fit the culture. Be specific rather than assuming. The package point matters most: if the candidate expects one number and the manager has heard another, the offer stage will fall apart. Send a written prep email after the call so they have it all in one place. Five minutes.
4: Wherever it’s possible, sequence your shortlist so the first interview is with a credible but not top-ranked candidate. Debrief them in detail and use what you learn to prepare the stronger candidates. Be clear on the line: every candidate you send must be someone you’d stand behind. Sending someone you know won’t get the job damages the client relationship and the candidate’s trust in us.
5: “Why do you want to work for us?” is one of the most common interview questions and one of the most common places interviews are lost. Rehearse it with the candidate. For objections, help them prepare a short, honest answer, never a cover story. The closing question gives the candidate a chance to handle any concern in the room, and gives you intel for the debrief. Ten minutes; have pairs practise the close.
6: Client prep is underrated and skipped by average recruiters. You know the candidate’s push and pull factors from your qualification call. Candidates know you’re selling to them, so they may not fully trust you; hearing the same thing from the hiring manager confirms it, makes them want the role more and builds your rapport. Example: if the candidate wants great benefits and the company has them, make sure the candidate hears it from the manager. Ten minutes.
7: Pre-close on every call, to the point where it feels repetitive. A consistent yes gives you something to reference at offer stage. If the answer shifts, the “what’s changed?” question uncovers a real reason, hardball, or lost interest. The power of silence is everything here: ask, then let them talk. If they say no with a genuine reason, you have an immediate reason to speak to the client and see if the objection can be overcome. Ten minutes; pairs practise the script.
8: Anything less than a 10 gives you material to prep the hiring manager with. On competing offers, find out what you’re up against and whether they have a favourite; the other companies are also business development leads. On counteroffers, ask how their employer will react, whether they’ve countered people before, and what, if anything, would make them stay. If they name something, ask: “Why should it take the threat of you leaving for you to get what you need?” Module 09 covers counteroffers in depth.
9: Momentum dies fast after an interview. Call the candidate as soon as they come out, and the client the same day. Always get a next step with a date from the client before you hang up; that’s client control (Module 07). Pass feedback both ways quickly and honestly. If you sent the weakest credible candidate first, this is where you collect the intel for the rest of the shortlist.
10: Groups of three. Brief the person playing the candidate privately: they have a competing offer that is slightly higher, but the other role is weaker on their main push factor. The trainee should uncover that through questions, not guess it. Success is a candidate who reaches their own decision, not one who feels pushed. Use the observer’s checklist for feedback.
11: Ask each person to apply the checklist to the live candidate they brought and name one thing they will do differently before that candidate’s next interview. Managers: listen in on one prep call and one pre-close call per person this week.
12: Open the floor for questions. Point to Module 09: handling counteroffers starts long before the offer, with the pre-close questions from today.
